title: A learner-free swarm reaches the explore-exploit equilibrium: A self-organized attractor approximating the reinforcement-learning solution
description: arXiv:2610.25113v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The explore-exploit trade-off is the core problem of reinforcement learning (RL). In its multi-agent, resource-sharing form the optimum is not a scalar-return maximum but an equilibrium allocation -- the ideal-free distribution (IFD), the Nash equilibrium of a congestion game. We show that a minimal foraging swarm reaches the shape of this equilibrium as a self-organized attractor -- foragers in proportion to resource richness (matching slope 0.94) -- with no learner, no trained parameters, and no payoff or reward read anywhere in its dynamics. Agents explore by heavy-tailed (Levy) flights, recruit neighbours to a discovery through a threshold cascade on their proximity network, and disperse as a patch crowds; removing the coupling of recruitment to movement collapses the matching (slope 0.08). The reinforcement learning is at the level of the problem and the allocation reached, not the micro-rule. The swarm reaches this equilibrium rather than learning it, attaining its shape but not the exact equilibrium: it stays measurably exploitable (Nash-gap 0.58 versus ~0.01 for a converged learner). Against PPO learners (feedforward, centralized-critic, and graph message-passing) trained in the same sensing-limited environment, the reward-free swarm at zero training matches the IFD gradient more faithfully than any learner (slope ~1 vs 0.69-0.91) and ties the best learner's harvest where clustered (both plateau at ~0.80 of an oracle ceiling), while the learner collects more where resource is scarce (0.33 vs 0.22) and holds tighter per-capita intake. Learning thus buys precision and transfer, not a better allocation; neither message passing nor a centralized critic exceeds it at this budget. We read this not as beating RL, but as evidence that a minimal swarm's physics reaches the equilibrium RL seeks without a learner, a reward, or a trained parameter. A companion paper develops the mechanism.

title: RADAgent: Automating RADseq Pipelines with Private Open-Source LLMs
description: arXiv:2610.33009v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Restriction site-associated DNA sequencing (RADseq) is a family of reduced-representation sequencing methods. It uses restriction enzymes to sample subsets of the genome, therefore allowing multiple individuals to be sequenced and genotyped together at low cost. RADseq is widely used for population genomics, evolutionary biology, marker discovery, and the development of SNP panels, but complete analysis still requires expert coordination across multiple tools and processing stages. Traditional RADseq analysis requires expert coordination of heterogeneous bioinformatics tools, intermediate artifacts, quality-control checks, and parameter-dependent decisions across multiple stages. Although individual steps can be scripted, executing the complete workflow still requires human oversight for state tracking, result validation, and failure handling. To automate this expert-driven coordination, we present RADAgent, which introduces a modular agentic method for reliable RADseq workflow execution with an open-weight LLM. RADAgent maps the natural boundaries of the RADseq workflow into 16 independently executable and verifiable agent modules and uses a model-independent runtime for bounded tool execution, on-disk verification, and failure recovery. We evaluate RADAgent on a real population-genomics dataset containing 476 samples from 19 populations. The results demonstrate that RADAgent reliably automates the complete RADseq workflow with an open-weight LLM while keeping genomic data and model execution within the local computing environment. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/wenlu-lab/RADAgent.

title: Same Story, Different Lens: A Multi-Agent System for Cross-Outlet News Framing Analysis
description: arXiv:2610.35208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: News outlets covering the same event differ in what they emphasize and omit. \textit{Same Story, Different Lens} is an experimental research prototype for comparing these choices. It collects world and politics coverage from 17 outlets, groups reports about the same event, and produces structured analyses of sentiment, political lean, framing, loaded language, possible omissions, and model-estimated proportions of factual claims and opinion. Loaded-language entries include quotations and neutral rewordings. Three model roles (agents) handle article analysis, assessment of source support, and cross-outlet briefing generation. Analyses are stored in a JSONL archive. The evaluation compares outlet-level lean estimates with approximate, predefined reference ratings and summarizes the Critic's model-assigned grounding scores. These measures provide preliminary diagnostics. A grounding score reflects the model's assessment of support in the supplied text and does not establish factual accuracy or constitute independent verification.

title: Aerial-R1: Reinforcing Aerial Reasoning and Segmentation in MLLMs
description: arXiv:2610.33056v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have revolutionized general visual perception, existing methods suffer from severe hallucination in the aerial domain, where extreme scale variations and visual ambiguity abound. Existing Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) paradigms force models to mimic ground truth without modeling uncertainty, often resulting in blind guessing on tiny or unrecognizable objects in aerial scenes. In this paper, we present Aerial-R1, the first aerial MLLM framework to reinforce visual reasoning capabilities for aerial reasoning and segmentation. Drawing inspiration from the reasoning-incentivizing mechanisms of DeepSeek-R1, we find that trustworthy perception stems from consistency across views, establishing a visual parallel to the Chain-of-Thought in logic. To effectively adapt policy optimization for non-autoregressive mask generation, we introduce Hybrid-View Group Advantage-Weighted Regression (H-GAWR). This strategy constructs dynamic groups of high-resolution and low-resolution views, seamlessly bridging group-relative advantage estimation with advantage-weighted policy extraction. By enforcing consensus on clear inputs and strictly penalizing hallucinations on ambiguous ones, Aerial-R1 develops an explicitly incentivized refusal mechanism. Extensive experiments on VSAI-Ref, the first aerial MLLM benchmark dedicated to jointly evaluating dense reasoning and hallucination robustness, demonstrate that Aerial-R1 significantly outperforms SFT baselines in segmentation precision while substantially mitigating fatal hallucinations in low-information scenarios, paving the way for more reliable and trustworthy aerial agents. Codes are available on https://github.com/phy709/Aerial-R1.

title: Improving the Chain-of-Thought Compressibility of Pruned Reasoning Models via Long--Short Contrastive Pruning
description: arXiv:2610.34336v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large reasoning models are costly to serve because they are large and because they generate long chains of thought (CoT). Weight pruning and CoT compression address these two costs separately, but they interfere in that pruning adds redundant reasoning on problems the model still solves and incomplete reasoning on those it no longer solves, and on harder problems makes the model less compressible by subsequent length-preference optimization. We trace this to a blind spot on each side: pruning criteria do not distinguish necessary from redundant reasoning, and preference-based CoT compression receives no training signal on problems a pruned model always or never solves. We propose Contrastive Set-Difference (CSD), which identifies neurons enriched in redundant reasoning by contrasting their activations on long and short correct solutions of the same problem and prunes them preferentially, and we extend preference pairs to the problems a pruned model always or never solves. Pruning 20\% of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, the combination uses 8--22\% fewer thinking tokens on four math benchmarks than pruning with reasoning-aware calibration (RAC) followed by the same compression, with accuracy within 0.5 points.

title: Bank of America kindly asks that you don’t share your banking password with your AI assistant
description: The banking giant reminds customers that "you're responsible for activity" resulting from your AI agents' access.
content: Financial giant Bank of America is reminding customers to bank safely by kindly not sharing your banking credentials with your AI agent. In an email blast to customers titled “Protecting your finances in the Al World,” Bank of America urged customers to never share their username and password with another person or an outside service, “including an Al-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf.” You can practically sense the frustration in the person sending the email. Still, customers are increasingly handing over their log-ins as personal AI assistants grow more popular . Sharing your banking username and password with an AI assistant runs the risk that it could do something with your finances without your knowledge, or that your bank thinks someone’s raiding your account and locks you out of it. Worse, a security flaw in the AI assistant could result in it leaking your banking credentials elsewhere, giving financially motivated hackers a way into your bank account. This latest warning comes as banks are still exploring how AI agents fit into the financial world but are reportedly grappling with unauthorized agents accessing their customers’ money . As we discussed onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt , banks, payment providers, and processors are still trying to figure out how to allow customers access to their bank accounts using AI tools, such as for agentic payments, which allow people to set agents to autonomously buy things at the best price or the right time. A spokesperson for Bank of America confirmed the authenticity of the bank’s email that was posted to social media . But heed the bank’s warning, for if things go wrong, it’s on you. Account agreements at most banks hold customers responsible for anyone they give their log-in to. “If you do share your credentials,” its email reads, “keep in mind that you’re responsible for activity resulting from that access.” (via Bryan Toporek ) Topics agentic payments , AI , Bank of America , Banking , cybersecurity , Fintech , Security When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . fingerprint: how to build a modern diffusion language model|arxiv.org/abs/2610.33391
title: How To Build A Modern Diffusion Language Model
description: arXiv:2610.33391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The frontier of large language model (LLM) performance has advanced rapidly in recent years, fueled by scaling laws for pretraining on large text corpora. However, mainstream LLMs have fundamental limitations: they generate text autoregressively, producing outputs sequentially from left to right one token at a time. This sequential process leaves parallel GPU hardware underutilized during inference--a bottleneck that has grown acute as progress shifts toward scaling post-training and inference-time compute--and commits irreversibly to each token without the ability to revise earlier mistakes. Discrete diffusion models address these limitations by generating tokens in parallel, starting from a noisy or masked sequence and iteratively refining the entire output over a series of denoising steps. This parallel generative process enables speeds of thousands of tokens per second, provides a new axis of inference-time compute scaling, and supports built-in error correction and controllable generation. Over the past two years, discrete diffusion has scaled to billions of parameters across biological sequence modeling and natural language, with open-weights and commercial releases from leading labs. This article provides a survey of key ideas in discrete diffusion and a high-level introduction to how modern diffusion LLMs are built, covering their foundations, core algorithmic and architectural building blocks, applications in biology and language, and implications for future LLM scaling laws.

title: How Reliable are AMR Parser Outputs? Uncertainty Estimation for AMR Parsing
description: arXiv:2610.13236v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent advances have significantly improved the performance of Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) parsers, yet determining when their outputs can be trusted remains largely unexplored. This work presents the first study of uncertainty estimation for AMR parsers in a black-box setting using top-k beam-search candidates. Uncertainty is estimated from pairwise candidate similarities and evaluated using the Prediction Rejection Ratio. This work characterises the relationship between parsing performance and uncertainty, evaluates the reliability of beam candidate distributions, analyses the effect of evaluation metrics on uncertainty assessment, and identifies parsers that provide the strongest balance between performance and reliability. Experimental results show the value of uncertainty estimation as a complementary dimension for evaluating AMR parsers.

title: Precedence-Aware Resource Allocation: Extending the AUTOC Framework to Multi-Level Treatments
description: arXiv:2610.34812v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many real-world decision problems require allocating limited resources across individuals to maximize total benefit often through interventions that vary in intensity rather than binary treat-or-not decisions. In these settings, higher levels treatments require first applying lower levels of treatment, inducing a precedence constraint that complicates allocation under a fixed budget. While the causal inference literature has largely emphasized accurate estimation of conditional average treatment effects (CATE), recent work has shown that estimation accuracy alone does not guarantee effective resource allocation, motivating ranking-based evaluation frameworks. The Area Under the Targeting Operating Characteristic (AUTOC) provides an effective way to evaluate prioritization rules across budget levels, but existing formulations are limited to binary treatments. We introduce Multi-Level AUTOC (ML-AUTOC), which is a generalization for AUTOC designed for multi-level treatment settings with precedence. We also propose precedence-aware policies for mapping true marginal treatment effects to feasible treatment assignments under fixed budget constraints. Our results show that in the setting of multi-level treatments, maximizing realized treatment effects may require re-allocation of treatments across individuals.

title: Evaluating LLM-based Agents for Multi-Turn Conversations: A Survey
description: arXiv:2503.22458v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This survey examines evaluation methods for large language model (LLM)-based agents in multi-turn conversational settings. Using a PRISMA-inspired framework, we systematically reviewed nearly 250 scholarly sources, capturing the state of the art from various venues of publication, and establishing a solid foundation for our analysis. Our study offers a structured approach by developing two interrelated taxonomy systems: one that defines \emph{what to evaluate} and another that explains \emph{how to evaluate}. The first taxonomy identifies key components of LLM-based agents for multi-turn conversations and their evaluation dimensions, including task completion, response quality, user experience, memory and context retention, as well as planning and tool integration. These components ensure that the performance of conversational agents is assessed in a holistic and meaningful manner. The second taxonomy system focuses on the evaluation methodologies. It categorizes approaches into annotation-based evaluations, automated metrics, hybrid strategies that combine human assessments with quantitative measures, and self-judging methods utilizing LLMs. This framework not only captures traditional metrics derived from language understanding, such as BLEU and ROUGE scores, but also incorporates advanced techniques that reflect the dynamic, interactive nature of multi-turn dialogues.

fingerprint: t2d target to draft model pruning adaptation for efficient speculative decoding|arxiv.org/abs/2610.34103
title: T2D: Target-to-Draft Model Pruning & Adaptation for Efficient Speculative Decoding
description: arXiv:2610.34103v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speculative decoding significantly accelerates autoregressive text generation in Large Language Models (LLMs), but its efficacy depends largely on two key factors: the distributional alignment between the draft and the target model, and the draft model's latency during inference. However, existing approaches typically utilize independently pretrained small draft models or seek to prune the target model to a manually chosen architecture, thereby failing to explicitly balance the trade-off between draft model alignment and token generation efficiency. To address this gap, we formulate draft model design as an optimization problem and propose T2D, a framework that constructs draft models directly from the target model using latency-aware structured pruning and knowledge distillation. In this manner, T2D obtains draft models that are jointly optimized for both measured inference latency and cross-entropy loss on the target model's responses, resulting in superlative speculative decoding performance. Through extensive experiments on multi-domain speculative decoding benchmarks and across several target model families of differing scale, we demonstrate how T2D prunes up to 92\% of the target model to obtain highly performant draft models compared to competitive baselines. Moreover, draft models obtained via T2D can also be utilized by other speculative decoding token-alignment and knowledge distillation methods in a plug-and-play fashion, leading to further gains. Our findings underscore the importance of jointly navigating the draft model architecture-alignment frontier to unlock the full potential of speculative decoding for LLMs.

title: Developer Task Delegation to LLMs and the Trust Factor: A Mixed Methods Study
description: arXiv:2610.34317v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: With the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs), software developers are presented with a powerful new approach: delegating software development tasks to LLMs. Existing studies have explored task delegation for a subset of tasks and factors. Critically, what tasks developers delegate to LLMs, to what extent, and why they delegate them, is not yet well understood. We explore these questions through 22 interviews and a survey with 160 software practitioners. Developers reported employing four modes of task delegation to LLMs: full delegation, partial delegation, self-delegation, and task avoidance. Drawing on our qualitative findings, we discuss the rationales behind these choices and explore how task difficulty, task risk, developer motivation, and trust appear to be associated with software development task delegation to LLMs. Our statistical analysis reveals that trust is a significant factor associated with task delegation to LLMs. Finally, we share actionable implications for human-AI collaboration in software research, and for software practitioners to make the most of their newly found powers of delegation.

title: $\xi$-DPO: Direct Preference Optimization via Ratio Reward Margin
description: arXiv:2605.10981v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reference-free preference optimization has emerged as an efficient alternative to reinforcement learning from human feedback, with Simple Preference Optimization(SimPO) demonstrating strong performance by eliminating the explicit reference model through a simple objective. However, the joint tuning of the hyperparameters $\beta$ and $\gamma$ in SimPO remains a central challenge. We argue that this difficulty arises because the margin formulation in SimPO is not easily interpretable across datasets with different reward gap structures. To better understand this issue, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of SimPO and find that $\beta$, rather than merely serving as a reward scaling factor, primarily functions to filter noisy samples, while the reward margin $\gamma$ defined by SimPO is not semantically well aligned with explicitly enlarging the reward gap between chosen and rejected responses. Motivated by these observations, we propose $\xi$-DPO: Direct preference optimization via ratio reward margin. We first reformulate the preference objective through an equivalent transformation, changing the optimization target from maximizing the likelihood of reward gaps to minimizing the distance between reward gaps and optimal margins. Then, we redefine the reward in a ratio form between the chosen and rejected, which effectively cancels the effect of $\beta$ and yields a bounded and interpretable margin. This margin is called the ratio reward margin and is denoted by $\xi$. Unlike the $\beta$ and $\gamma$ in SimPO, $\xi$ can be determined from the initial reward gap distribution, thus much easier to tune. Our extensive experimental results show that $\xi$-DPO substantially outperforms existing preference optimization methods across open benchmarks on multiple evaluation metrics.

title: Difference-in-Differences on a Censored Rating Scale Can Manufacture an Effect: Evidence from a Pre-Registered LLM-Judge Audit
description: arXiv:2608.27309v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM-judge audits assess bias by comparing ratings across matched conditions. Difference-in-differences designs take the rating difference between two candidate responses to each item and compare it across a manipulated attribute. Building on prior work on nonlinear difference-in-differences, we show in closed form that when ratings are bounded, a severity shift common to both responses produces an observed interaction whenever the scale bounds attenuate it unequally. We then report a pre-registered audit of 990 calls to a frozen pedagogy judge. The registered primary analysis did not detect an effect of a stated novice or advanced profile on scaffolding preference. The only nominally significant secondary interaction was on the productive-struggle sub-score ($+0.378$ points; $p = 0.002$). A post-hoc construction with zero differential preference reproduced 79 to 85% of this interaction using the observed severity shift and the scale floor alone. The observed interaction therefore does not identify differential preference on the latent scale.

description: arXiv:2602.00996v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Complex question answering across text, tables and images requires integrating diverse information sources. It uses specialized agents: Table, Context, Visual, Summarizing and Verification, that communicate through a shared natural-language log as persistent memory. title: MAGNET: Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network for Connectome Generation
description: arXiv:2610.17014v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Functional brain connectome represents neural connectivity as a matrix of pairwise interactions between brain regions. Generation of functional connectomes is not only a question of validity; rather, having satisfied the constraints on the correlation matrix, the next step is to recover the class-conditional geometry buried under coarse labels. We propose MAGNET, a Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network which uses a normalized-Cholesky representation of the manifold of correlation matrices that guarantees validity. MAGNET lifts noisy latent states into ROI-level region tokens and performs denoising with a relational inductive bias over brain atlas regions. To deal with structural problems induced by coarse labels, MAGNET employs class-anchored conditioning, amortized structural bridge, and relevance-preserving corruption. Across ABIDE, ADNI, and OASIS-3, MAGNET consistently achieves favorable results compared to previous manifold-aware approaches, demonstrating improvements of 7-21% in class-conditional fidelity ($\alpha,\beta$-F1) across three cohorts and better sampling efficiency. Moreover, while training only with strict binary labels, MAGNET is capable of maintaining clinical heterogeneity through fine substructure of the connectomes in a zero-shot setting, improving subclass covariance alignment ($\lambda$-MSE) by over 30%. These results suggest that geometric validity is a necessary but insufficient condition for clinical utility in connectome synthesis. Moreover, efforts in making the diffusion denoising class-conditional manifold aware finds utility beyond the highly curved brain connectome generation as this is a critical problem in various general settings. The code repository can be found at https://github.com/protyayofficial/MAGNET.

title: Multi-Agent Debate for Belief Optimization in Defeasible Domains
description: arXiv:2605.12718v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-agent debate has emerged as a promising approach for improving LLM reasoning on ground-truth tasks, yet current methodologies face certain structural limitations: debate tends to induce a martingale over belief trajectories, majority voting accounts for most observed gains, and LLMs exhibit confidence escalation rather than calibration across rounds. We argue that the genuine value of debate, and dialectic systems as a whole, lies not in ground-truth tasks but in defeasible domains, where every position can in principle be defeated by better reasoning. We present the Council of Hierarchical Agentic Language (CHAL), a multi-agent dialectic framework that treats defeasible argumentation as an engine for belief optimization. Each agent maintains a CHAL Belief Schema (CBS), a graph-structured belief representation with a Bayesian-inspired architecture, that facilitates belief revision through a gradient-informed dynamic mechanism by leveraging the strength of the belief's thesis as a differentiable objective. Meta-cognitive value systems spanning epistemology, logic, and ethics are elevated to configurable hyperparameters governing agent reasoning and adjudication outcomes. We provide a series of ablation experiments that demonstrate systematic and interpretable effects: the adjudicator's value system determines the debate's overall trajectories in latent belief space, council diversity refines beliefs for all participants, and the framework generalizes across broad fields. CHAL is, to our knowledge, the first framework to treat multi-agent debate as structured belief optimization over defeasible domains. Further, the auditable belief artifacts it produces establish the foundation for dedicated evaluation suites for defeasible argumentation, with broader implications for building AI systems whose reasoning and value commitments are transparent, aligned, and subject to human oversight.

title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling
description: arXiv:2610.35464v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning models are now widely used to predict environmental variable dynamics in domains like hydrology, climate science, agriculture, and ecology. These models are usually compared on fixed benchmark datasets using a single average accuracy score. As models improve, their scores become very close when averaged over large regions and long time periods, so the benchmark can no longer tell them apart, and a single number hides \emph{where} and \emph{when} a model fails. Three failures are common across environmental domains: models get worse as the climate shifts (non-stationarity), models fail at unmonitored sites (spatial extrapolation), and models miss rare but important regimes such as floods and droughts. We present \textbf{EvoBench}, a benchmark framework that shows where a model fails, tracks failures over time, and evolves to focus on model capability gaps. We apply EvoBench to daily streamflow prediction as a case study (\textbf{CAMELS-Evolve}, about 9{,}000 U.S. basins, 1985--2024) and compare an operational physical model (NWM), a conceptual reference (HBV), and several data-driven models. No model wins on every testing scenarios (e.g., in terms of average accuracy, performance at low flows and unmonitored basins). Also we observe that all data-driven models under-predict floods. Additionally, we show that targeted fix based on the reported failures could mitigate weaknesses the benchmark identified in certain scenarios. EvoBench turns model evaluation from a saturated ranking into a moving map of model limitations.

title: SRA: Selective Residual Adaptation for LLM Reasoning Enhancement
description: arXiv:2610.34199v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers reasoning capabilities from large language models to lightweight students. However, distilled small models still struggle with multi-step reasoning. We observe that the distribution divergences between teacher and student models along reasoning paths are highly sparse, and target tokens almost always fall within the student top-$K$ candidate set. Based on this finding, unlike approaches updating student backbones or requiring runtime teacher computation, we propose Selective Residual Adaptation (SRA), a plug-and-play framework that internalizes localized corrections. Concretely, SRA employs a Discrepancy Gate to identify divergence positions alongside a Candidate Residual Adapter for top-$K$ logit calibration to correct the mismatch. Theoretically, we establish error bounds ensuring strict sequence level performance gains. Across mathematical benchmarks on Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 4B, SRA consistently enhances distilled student models, raising average Pass@16 by up to 4.37 percentage points while preserving general capabilities.

title: HealthAgentBench: A Unified Benchmark Suite of Realistic Agentic Healthcare Environments for Challenging Frontier AI Agents
description: arXiv:2606.31179v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As AI agents become increasingly capable of complex, long-horizon reasoning, rigorous evaluation is essential for measuring progress toward real-world healthcare applications. However, existing healthcare benchmarks are often static or narrow in clinical scope, motivating broader evaluation of agents acting on raw patient data. We introduce HealthAgentBench, a suite of 75 agentic healthcare tasks across 9 categories each with its unique environment. The benchmark suite spans diagnosis, specimen assessment, research, and data management workflows and a broad range of modalities. Each task is designed to replicate an end-to-end clinical workflow: given task instructions and supporting resources, an agent must explore raw healthcare data, operate within a complex environment, and execute multi-step solutions that go beyond naive prompting, such as querying large clinical databases or interpreting gigapixel pathology images. All tasks are scored using binary success criteria derived from reference labels, executable rules, or computational baselines. We evaluate six agents (three GPT models through Codex and three Claude models through Claude Code) with one scored attempt per task (450 evaluations). Overall success ranges from 32.0% to 57.3%; Claude Code Opus-5.5 leads with a 57.3% success rate, followed by GPT-6-astra and Sonnet-5.5 at 50.7% each. Performance varies substantially by category with specialized imaging modalities such as CT and MRI being especially difficult. HealthAgentBench provides a challenging and realistic benchmark with substantial room for future progress. We release our benchmark athttps://github.com/microsoft/HealthAgentBench.

title: CodeMeepo: A Multi-Agent Workflow for Repository-Level Code Migration and Optimization
description: arXiv:2610.34633v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Repository-level code migration rewrites an entire project in a new programming language while preserving its observable behavior. It is challenging because behavior spans interdependent modules, dependencies and build infrastructure must be adapted to the target ecosystem, and the source code is often the only specification. Large language model agents can now attempt these migrations end to end, but three challenges remain. First, an agent that writes both the translation and its acceptance tests may overlook the same requirements in both, leaving missing or incorrect behavior undetected. Second, large repositories can exceed a model's context window, and dividing the work into smaller tasks does not ensure that all required behavior is migrated. Third, even behaviorally correct translations may be slower than the original implementation. We present CodeMeepo, a multi-agent pipeline for complete and efficient migration of large repositories. Each milestone is evaluated against a fixed external oracle that the agents neither author nor modify. A separate parity assessment compares source and target components in scope and adds identified gaps back into the plan as required work. Ordered milestones limit the scope of each task, while cumulative regression checks guard against breaking already-migrated behavior. A benchmark-guided optimization phase addresses performance, followed by full-suite conformance testing and repair. Eight specialized agent roles communicate through file artifacts, and a deterministic state machine governs repair, deferral, scope changes, and termination. On nine subjects in three language pairs, CodeMeepo achieves the best pass rate on every subject and passes 18% more tests than a state-of-the-art multi-agent baseline using the same model. On a production daemon, its optimization phase improves half of the benchmarks, by 25% on average.

title: Folding Pooled Usage Examples into the Tool Index Lowers Retrieval of Unused Tools
description: arXiv:2610.30867v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI agents often find tools by searching their documentation. Agents that share a tool catalog can also pool usage examples: past requests, each tagged with the tool that handled it. We ask what pooling does to tools no agent has used yet. Adding each usage example to the search index as an extra entry for its tool (folding) helps tools that have examples, but on two of three catalogs it sharply lowers how often a needed unused tool reaches the top five results; on StableToolBench with our main embedding model, the share falls from 73 to 40 percent of queries. When the extra entries hold documentation from other tools instead of requests, the loss is much smaller, though differences in content or writing style could also explain this. We introduce ZoE (Z-scores over Evidence), a scoring rule that scores the documentation and the usage of a tool separately, so a tool without usage keeps its documentation score. On all three catalogs and with both embedding models we tested, ZoE retrieves unused tools more often than a router that reserves result slots for usage matches. With our main embedding model, the router retrieves more of the other tools on two catalogs, and in post hoc comparisons a simpler rule that adds a constant to the scores of tools with usage shows no detected difference from ZoE on unused tools. For five simulated agents on one catalog, folding lowered retrieval of unused tools for every agent; with ZoE no average drop was detected, though some agents still lost. Evaluations of pooled agent experience should report tools no agent has used separately from the average.

title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
description: arXiv:2610.35862v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many everyday tasks require controlling contact force as well as motion. On a humanoid, this force must often be coordinated across both hands and the whole body, and cannot be specified by kinematic trajectories alone. Therefore, we present FLORE, a framework for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation. We collect robot-free demonstrations using two force-sensing UMI-style handheld grippers for hand motion and contact wrenches, and wearable trackers for body motion. A force-reactive diffusion policy takes vision, proprioception, and measured wrenches as input, then predicts actions and per-hand force commands. A hybrid compliance whole-body controller with force tracking executes these commands while maintaining balance: an integral of the force error measured by real force/torque (F/T) sensors lets each hand track force accurately along the commanded direction and remain compliant along the others. In simulation, the controller tracks per-hand force commands of varied magnitude and direction, with little loss in whole-body motion accuracy. Across three contact-rich tasks on the robot, the force-reactive policy succeeds in 80% of rollouts, compared with 26.7% for a position-only policy trained on the same demonstrations and executed by the same controller. For more details, please visit our website: https://louis-leee.github.io/FLoRe/.

description: arXiv:2608.19760v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Step-level credit evaluation can conflate numerical association with ordering and branch recovery with position-selection value. title: Efficient Exact Unlearning for Federated Zeroth-Order Optimization
description: arXiv:2610.35211v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Federated zeroth-order optimization (FedZOO) reduces the memory and communication costs of collaborative training for edge intelligence by avoiding backpropagation while communicating only random seeds and scalar coefficients. However, existing methods lack efficient mechanisms for exact unlearning to fully remove the influence of training data when users request deletion. A key insight is that total variation stability of the learning algorithm creates overlap between model distributions before and after data deletion, allowing exact unlearning to reuse computation through coupling. Based on this observation, we jointly design two stable zeroth-order learning algorithms and their corresponding exact-unlearning procedures: \textsc{FedZOO-S} obtains stability through client and mini-batch subsampling, enabling \textsc{FedZOUL-S} to perform efficient unlearning by preserving earlier updates and restarting from the first affected step. \textsc{FedZOO-NS} further combines subsampling with Gaussian noise to increase overlap between update distributions; \textsc{FedZOUL-NS} exploits this overlap through rejection--reflection coupling to reuse affected updates when the coupling is accepted. We prove exact unlearning for both algorithms: the model and saved state have the same joint distribution as retraining with the corresponding learner on retained data. We further establish stability and convergence guarantees for the learning algorithms and derive upper bounds on expected unlearning cost. Experiments demonstrate effective unlearning with competitive model utility and up to $56.1\%$ less cumulative unlearning time than re-optimization. Compared with first-order baselines, our methods reduce communication overhead by up to approximately four orders of magnitude.

title: Disruptive raises $10B fund to make big bets on at least 10 companies
description: Disruptive has made headlines in recent years for pouring money into companies like chip startup Groq and the AI voice-generation startup ElevenLabs.
content: In Brief Posted: 11:55 AM PDT · October 27, 2026 Image Credits: Altayb (opens in a new window) / Getty Images Dominic-Madori Davis Disruptive raises $10B fund to make big bets on at least 10 companies The Dallas-based investment firm Disruptive, whose past bets include Palantir, Airbnb, and Spotify, announced a $10 billion fund to back at least 10 late-stage companies, with checks of up to $1 billion, it said Tuesday . It’s one of the biggest fundraises of the year so far, aiming to back (what else?!) the capital-intensive fields of AI and defense. The Wall Street Journal first reported earlier this month that the firm was seeking to raise the fund and by then had already secured at least $7.5 billion in capital commitments. The firm was founded in 2012 by Alex Davis, grandson of billionaire oil magnate Marvin Davis. This is technically the firm’s first blind-pool fund, meaning investors commit money without knowing which companies it will back. Until now, the firm raised money through deal-by-deal special purpose vehicles . Disruptive has nonetheless made headlines in recent years for pouring money into companies like chip startup Groq and the AI voice-generation startup ElevenLabs. Bloomberg reported that the firm told LPs it has returned more than $6 billion on the roughly $1.9 billion it has put into startups. According to the Dallas Business Journal, the new vehicle is the largest venture fund raised in Texas history. title: Crazyflow: An Accurate, GPU-Accelerated, Differentiable Drone Simulator in JAX
description: arXiv:2606.01478v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: High-quality, large-scale synthetic data from simulations is becoming a cornerstone for pushing robots' capabilities. While aerial robotics simulators have evolved to support specialized needs such as fidelity, differentiability, and swarms independently, a unified platform that synthesizes data across all these domains is missing. In this work, we propose Crazyflow, a simulator designed to push the frontier of aerial robotics algorithm development, supporting model-based and data-driven methods, gradient-based and sampling-based approaches, single- and multi-agent systems, and state- and vision-based policy learning. Crazyflow combines high-fidelity dynamics with JAX for speed and differentiability, scaling to millions of environments or thousands of swarms with thousands of drones on single CPUs and GPUs, and beyond on clusters. Real-world experiments show Crazyflow supports both analytical-gradient-based policy learning, achieving high-accuracy tracking without domain randomization, and sampling-based obstacle avoidance at speeds exceeding half a billion steps per second. Breaking the traditional train-then-deploy paradigm, Crazyflow's performance enables in-flight reinforcement learning; we demonstrate this by throwing a physical drone into the air and training a recovery policy from scratch in 0.37 seconds, catching it before it hits the ground. By pushing accuracy, speed, and differentiability simultaneously, Crazyflow serves as an open-source resource for synthetic data generation, with emerging capabilities for large-scale parallelization for online, in-execution learning and optimization, opening the door to novel algorithm development.

fingerprint: matching matters a fair quality efficiency benchmark for command line agents|arxiv.org/abs/2606.21140
title: Matching Matters: A Fair Quality-Efficiency Benchmark for Command-Line Agents
description: arXiv:2606.21140v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Rapid advances in large language models have improved the task-solving capabilities of command-line-interface (CLI)-based agents, whose CLIs determine how models invoke tools, maintain interaction history, and recover from failures. Consequently, effective matching between CLIs and LLMs has become essential. However, existing agent benchmarks largely emphasize success rate while overlooking practical objectives such as cost and efficiency, as well as the selection of LM-CLI combinations, all of which are critical in real-world deployment. We therefore introduce AgentMeter, a quality-efficiency benchmark with a new metric, the AgentMeter Score (AMS), that jointly characterizes task quality, budget sensitivity, and resource-intensive zero-reward execution, enabling a more complete assessment of deployed LM-CLI pairs. Furthermore, collected task descriptions may inadvertently favor LM-CLI pairs that are particularly compatible with their wording and structure, causing evaluation results to reflect description-specific advantages rather than general task-solving capability. We therefore propose AgentMeter-Opt, a trajectory-grounded optimization framework that constructs pair-adapted, task-preserving description variants to build a fairer evaluation set across LM-CLI pairs. Extensive experiments show that no CLI is universally optimal across language models and that task success, execution cost, and AMS identify different competitive configurations. Results on AgentMeter-Opt further reveal that task-preserving description changes affect LM-CLI pairs unevenly and can alter their relative ordering across valid description conditions. Together, AgentMeter and AgentMeter-Opt provide a practical foundation for fair and deployment-relevant evaluation of command-line agents.

title: GUIFlow: Temporal Redundancy-Aware Incremental Inference for GUI Agents
description: arXiv:2610.34959v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GUI agents built on vision-language models interact with continuously evolving interfaces, yet conventional inference repeatedly recomputes representations of largely overlapping observations and histories. This mismatch makes multi-step interaction costly, while changes in context, interface content, and action arguments prevent straightforward cache reuse. We introduce GUIFlow, a framework for full-pipeline incremental inference in multi-image GUI interaction. Our central insight is that advancing a decision need not require rebuilding all supporting representations: each interaction step can instead selectively update computational states maintained across the trajectory. To support new decisions as the context evolves, GUIFlow adapts how past computation is reused: historical KV states are position-aligned and injected into the current context; change signals guide selective updates of current-observation states in the vision encoder and language model; and earlier action responses serve as speculative drafts verified by the target model. Together, these mechanisms enable cross-step reuse throughout visual encoding, prefill, and decoding without additional training, a separate draft model, or changes to the model-visible inputs and action interface. Experiments demonstrate up to 3.39x geometric-mean speedup across offline multi-image benchmarks and up to 3.49x in online, closed-loop interaction on OSWorld, while maintaining task performance broadly comparable to the dense baseline.

title: Counterfactual Model Testing Under Distribution Shift
description: arXiv:2610.33594v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deployed machine learning (ML) models can degrade as the distribution of their input data shifts. Such shifts can result from changes in the population or from data integrity issues in the pipeline that materializes model features, two sources that operate through different mechanisms. Because labels are often absent or delayed, it is common practice to track shifts in the data instead, but a detected shift does not indicate how it affects the model. We formulate this problem as online model testing under distribution shift. Testing requires reproducing the shift on a controlled baseline with known labels. Since the same shift can come from either source, doing so requires knowing which mechanism changed. We propose a methodology that reproduces observed changes in both mechanisms to estimate current performance and the potential gain from repairing observed data integrity issues. Experiments on real-world datasets with simulated faults show that separating the two sources generally improves both estimates, supporting this formulation. A churn prediction case illustrates how these tests can support monitoring and repair prioritization

title: DRA-SAM: Disagreement-Driven Referential Active SAM for Low-Altitude Drone Referring Segmentation
description: arXiv:2610.33057v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Referring segmentation in low-altitude drone imagery requires distinguishing small, visually similar instances under complex linguistic and spatial constraints. Global inference may yield multiple plausible masks or leave the intended referent insufficiently represented, motivating selective local re-inference. We propose DRA-SAM, a disagreement-driven framework that allocates an additional inference pass according to competing referential hypotheses and an unresolved state. A lightweight EvidenceScorer estimates beliefs over existing candidates and the unresolved state. A training-free Referential Disagreement LOOK policy balances belief-weighted candidate competition and unresolved-region coverage to select a crop for local re-inference. The same benchmark-adapted SAM3-I backbone processes the selected region, and the resulting evidence updates existing hypotheses and introduces new candidates. Among the compared methods, DRA-SAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on six of seven test metrics on both RIS-LAD and UAVid-RIS, including mIoU and P@0.5-P@0.9, and on all seven RIS-LAD validation metrics. On RIS-LAD, DRA-SAM improves the matched global SAM3-I baseline from 49.55 to 52.34 mIoU and from 46.80 to 58.05 P@0.5. On UAVid-RIS, the independently adapted DRA-SAM achieves 73.26 mIoU and 86.86 P@0.5. Controlled crop-policy comparisons demonstrate the effectiveness of disagreement-guided crop selection, while target-size analysis reveals particularly pronounced gains for aerial targets occupying less than 1% of an image. These results establish referential disagreement as an effective criterion for allocating local inference. Code is available at https://github.com/phy709/DRA-SAM.

title: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3
content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3 Team Article Published October 27, 2026 Upvote 44 +38 Leonie Monigatti iamleonie Follow LiquidAI Jimmy T.H. Smith jimmysmith1919 Follow LiquidAI Anthony Maltsev amaltsev Follow LiquidAI Maxime Labonne mlabonne Follow LiquidAI Brandon Brandon3967 Follow LiquidAI Samuel Stevens samuelstevens Follow LiquidAI Ryan Shubert shubeydoo Follow LiquidAI Tianshu Yu tianshu-yu Follow LiquidAI Sina s-jse Follow LiquidAI Tim Seyde tseyde Follow LiquidAI Rouzbeh Amin Tafreshi rouzbehat78 Follow LiquidAI Alexander Amini alexanderamini Follow LiquidAI Saniya Karwa saniyakarwa Follow LiquidAI Marc Harkonen haerski Follow LiquidAI Anna Piunova orech Follow LiquidAI Calder Katyal CalderKat Follow LiquidAI Ishwarya Ananthabhotla ianant93 Follow LiquidAI Farris Atif farris-liquid Follow LiquidAI Tarek Dakhran tdakhran Follow LiquidAI Paul Pak paulpak58 Follow LiquidAI xx tugot17 Follow LiquidAI Mihir Bafna mihirbafna Follow LiquidAI Kyle Bruce Wheeler m3m0ryh0l3 Follow LiquidAI Aditya Tadimeti adityatadimeti Follow LiquidAI Alfred Eng alfredeng Follow LiquidAI Karthik Macherla karthikrmacherla Follow LiquidAI Khoi Nguyen KTLK Follow LiquidAI Aldo Gael Carranza agcarranza Follow LiquidAI Aurelien Lac Aurelien-Lac Follow LiquidAI Tyler Murray undfined Follow LiquidAI Raahul Vignesh Raahul26 Follow LiquidAI Song Duong sduong Follow LiquidAI Ramin Hasani raminmh Follow LiquidAI Mathias Lechner mlech26l Follow LiquidAI Akhilesh Deepak Gotmare akhileshdeepakgotmare Follow LiquidAI Fernando Fernandes Neto fernandofernandes Follow LiquidAI Jiahui Wang WWWjiahui Follow LiquidAI Yuri Khrustalev ykhrustalev Follow LiquidAI Alay Shah alay2shah Follow LiquidAI Simon Lee yungisimon Follow LiquidAI Mayank Agarwal mayankagarwal Follow LiquidAI Zetian Li zetianli Follow LiquidAI changyi yang changyiyang Follow LiquidAI Sinoué GAD GAD-cell Follow LiquidAI nathan ranchin nathanrchn Follow LiquidAI :last-child]:mb-0"> LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs. LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family: More capability per parameter: a new tri-hybrid architecture and training recipe allow LFM3-1.7B to outperform LFM2.5-2.6B while using 35% fewer parameters. Every modality on one backbone: six 2B-class models (text, vision, audio, omni, and decision) trained from LFM3-1.7B-Base, including our first omni model and video input for our vision model. Built for the edge: the text model fits in about 1 GB at 4-bit precision, new in-house vision and audio encoders speed up processing, and the text model’s 256K context window lets agents run on-device. Made to be specialized: every model fine-tunes on a single GPU, so you can adapt it to your data, terminology, and deployment environment. How we built a more expressive backbone LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU. LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes: Tri-hybrid layer mix: 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention (SWA) layers with a 256-token window, and 6 global attention layers. The convolutions use a kernel size of 7, up from 3 in LFM2. Head-wise gated attention: a sigmoid gate scales each head's output, so a head can switch off when it has nothing to add. This can help suppress activation outliers that hurt quantization. Partial RoPE: global attention layers rotate only the highest-frequency half of each head, so the other half matches on content regardless of distance. SWA layers keep full RoPE. Sandwich norm: each block normalizes both its input and its output to keep activations well-scaled. The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B . The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens. One backbone for six models Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device. Model Input Output Built on LFM3-1.7B Text Text LFM3-1.7B-Base LFM3-VL-2B Text, images, video Text LFM3 backbone + vision encoder LFM3-Audio-2B Text, audio Text, speech LFM3 backbone + audio encoder, audio decoder, and LiquidCodec LFM3-Omni-2B Text, images, video, audio Text, speech LFM3 backbone + vision and audio encoders and audio decoder d1-2B Text, images, video Calibrated answers LFM3-VL-2B d1-omni-2B Text, images, video, audio Calibrated answers LFM3-Omni-2B The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders: Vision encoder: it combines convolution and attention and uses 3x less compute than the SigLIP2 encoder in previous LFM VL models. Our 164M-parameter encoder matches Qwen3.5-2B's vision encoder in accuracy while requiring 2.2x fewer FLOPs (both measured with the same LFM2.5-230M language backbone). For video, it embeds each pair of sampled frames into one temporal slice, halving the temporal sequence length. Audio encoder and LiquidCodec: the audio encoder mixes sliding-window attention and short convolutions and is fully causal, so the model can prefill while you speak, with time to first token as low as 50 ms. LiquidCodec, our new audio tokenizer, turns generated tokens into speech at about 87x real time on a single CPU thread on Apple M4 Max and supports streaming decoding. How to use the LFM3 models Each model runs in transformers . The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports. LFM3-1.7B Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card . To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers : pip install -U transformers Then load and run the model: from transformers import pipeline generator = pipeline( "text-generation" , model= "LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B" , trust_remote_code= True , ) messages = [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is C. elegans?" }] output = generator( messages, do_sample= True , temperature= 0.1 , top_k= 50 , repetition_penalty= 1.1 , max_new_tokens= 2048 , ) print (output[ 0 ][ "generated_text" ][- 1 ][ "content" ]) For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide . LFM3-VL-2B Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card . To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.21.0" torch torchvision pillow Then load and run the model: import torch from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B" model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map= "auto" , trust_remote_code= True ) processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "url" : "https://placecats.com/300/200" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Describe this image." }, ], } ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, do_sample= True , temperature= 0.1 , top_k= 50 , repetition_penalty= 1.1 , max_new_tokens= 16384 , # generate() needs an explicit limit; reasoning can be long ) generated_ids = output_ids[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] :] print (processor.batch_decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens= True )[ 0 ]) See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp. LFM3-Audio-2B Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card . To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch accelerate librosa soundfile Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub: import torch import soundfile as sf from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B" device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32 model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code= True ). eval () processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device). eval () Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech: conversation = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "Respond with interleaved text and audio." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : [{ "type" : "audio" , "audio" : "question.wav" }]}, { "role" : "assistant" , "content" : "<|mixed_start|>" }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, continue_final_message= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(device) with torch.no_grad(): outputs = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens= 1024 , audio_temperature= 1.0 , audio_top_k= 128 , audio_repetition_penalty= 1.1 , audio_repetition_window= 4096 , return_dict_in_generate= True , ) text = processor.decode( outputs.sequences[ 0 , inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:], skip_special_tokens= True , ) waveform = codec.decode( outputs.audio_codes[: 1 , :, :outputs.audio_lengths[ 0 ]] ).audio_values[ 0 ] # 24 kHz print (text) sf.write( "reply.wav" , waveform. float ().cpu().numpy(), 24_000 ) See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling. LFM3-Omni-2B Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card . To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch torchvision torchcodec accelerate pillow librosa soundfile import torch import soundfile as sf from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Omni-2B" device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32 model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code= True ). eval () processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device). eval () Then ask a question about a photo by voice: conversation = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "Answer questions about the provided image. Base every answer only on what can be seen. Respond with text." , }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : "photo.jpg" }, { "type" : "audio" , "audio" : "question.wav" }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(device) with torch.no_grad(): outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 1024 , generation_mode= "text" ) print (processor.decode( outputs.sequences[ 0 , inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:outputs.sequence_lengths[ 0 ]], skip_special_tokens= True , )) See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling. d1-2B and d1-omni-2B Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B . Between the two d1 models: d1-2B : choose it for text, pictures, and video. It replaces d1-3B with a third fewer parameters and scores higher on all four of our decision suites, for example, 75.5 against 64.0 on ImajevBench. d1-omni-2B : choose it when your inputs include audio. If you ask by voice instead of in writing, it keeps nearly all of its accuracy. To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.19" torch torchvision pillow Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass: import torch from transformers import AutoModel device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.float32 if device == "cpu" else torch.bfloat16 model = AutoModel.from_pretrained( "LiquidAI/d1-2B" , trust_remote_code= True , dtype=dtype).to(device) # Several named questions over one state, answered in one pass questions = { "refund" : { "type" : "noul" , "instructions" : "Is the customer asking for a refund?" }, # yes/no: P(yes) "team" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Charges, refunds, invoices" , "shipping" : "Delivery and parcels" , "technical" : "App or site faults" }}, "topics" : { "type" : "choice" , "multiple" : True , "instructions" : "Which topics does the message raise?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and charges" , "delivery" : "Shipping and parcels" , "login" : "Signing in to the account" }}, "urgency" : { "type" : "score" , "instructions" : "How urgent is this ticket?" , "criteria" : [ "low" , "medium" , "high" ]}, } out = model.system_one( "I was charged twice and my parcel never arrived. Please refund one charge." , questions) a = out[ "answers" ] urgency = a[ "urgency" ][ "legend" ][ str ( int (a[ "urgency" ][ "score" ]))] print ( round (a[ "refund" ][ "noul" ], 2 ), a[ "team" ][ "choice" ], a[ "topics" ][ "choices" ], urgency) # 1.0 billing ['billing', 'delivery'] medium For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions. Fine-tune LFM3 for your task LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud. Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation. Model Method Task Notebook LFM3-1.7B SFT Extract structured JSON from messy documents Open in Colab LFM3-1.7B DPO Answer from retrieved documents, or decline Open in Colab LFM3-1.7B GRPO Call the right tools in a 108-tool phone app Open in Colab LFM3-1.7B CPT Learn a new language (Turkish) from raw text Open in Colab LFM3-VL-2B SFT Read receipt photos into JSON Open in Colab LFM3-VL-2B GRPO Transcribe images of equations to LaTeX Open in Colab LFM3-Audio-2B SFT Map spoken smart-home commands to function calls Open in Colab LFM3-Audio-2B SFT Teach the model a new voice Open in Colab LFM3-Omni-2B SFT Map spoken smart-home commands to function calls Open in Colab LFM3-Omni-2B SFT Answer spoken questions about medical images Open in Colab Example: teaching LFM3 to act We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation . The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware. Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video . Get Started with LFM3 All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today: Download: the LFM3 collection on Hugging Face, including LFM3-1.7B-Base for your own post-training. Fine-tune: adapt LFM3 to your task with our fine-tuning notebooks . Use in your harness: follow our guide on how to run a local agent, like OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and Pi. We can't wait to see what you build. fingerprint: do mllms really see it reinforcing visual attention in multimodal llms|arxiv.org/abs/2602.08241
title: Do MLLMs Really See It: Reinforcing Visual Attention in Multimodal LLMs
description: arXiv:2602.08241v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has substantially improved multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on complex reasoning tasks, existing approaches largely rely on long textual reasoning trajectories and provide limited mechanisms for learning stable visual attention policies. Our analysis shows that current MLLMs exhibit weak visual focus: early-stage visual misalignment is rarely corrected during subsequent reasoning, leading to error propagation and failed inferences. We argue that this limitation stems from inadequate credit assignment for visual attention during training. To address this issue, we propose SAYO, a visual reasoning model trained with a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that introduces a region-level visual attention-based reward. This reward explicitly aligns optimization signals with visually grounded reasoning steps, enabling the model to learn more reliable attention behaviors. Extensive experiments across multiple multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that SAYO consistently improves performance on diverse reasoning and perception tasks. Project is open at https://github.com/Cratileo/Sayo.

fingerprint: prefer personalized review summarization with online preference learning|arxiv.org/abs/2605.05911
title: PREFER: Personalized Review Summarization with Online Preference Learning
description: arXiv:2605.05911v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Product reviews significantly influence purchasing decisions on e-commerce platforms. However, the sheer volume of reviews can overwhelm users, obscuring information most relevant to their individual needs. Existing e-commerce summarization systems typically produce generic, static summaries that fail to account for the fact that (i) different users prioritize different product characteristics, and (ii) these preferences may evolve with interactions. To address these challenges, we propose an online learning framework that generates personalized summaries for each user by representing user interests in a latent aspect space and selecting preference-aligned review evidence. Our system then iteratively refines its understanding of user preferences by incorporating feedback on the generated summaries directly over time. We evaluate our framework on Amazon Reviews'23 using controlled feedback simulations and robustness checks with held-out-history, independent-embedding, and external LLM-based evaluators. These experiments show improvements in preference-aligned evidence selection under the evaluated feedback settings. A separate human-based study finds that scenario-conditioned summaries are preferred over generic (uniformly-aggregated) alternatives in 69.9% of paired comparisons.

fingerprint: towards practical algorithm selection for unsupervised domain adaptation in medical imaging|arxiv.org/abs/2607.28125
title: Towards Practical Algorithm Selection for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation in Medical Imaging
description: arXiv:2607.28125v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Numerous unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) algorithms exist, but for clinical practice, selecting the best-suited one along with proper hyperparameters often remains unclear, as the unlabeled deployment (target) domain prevents direct evaluation. We propose a label-free criterion that jointly selects the algorithm and hyperparameters for UDA. Given a pool of candidate models from multiple algorithms trained with different hyperparameters, our approach scores each candidate against an agreement reference, and selects the one with the highest score. The agreement reference is constructed in two levels without using target labels. First, we leverage multiple label-free selection signals, using each to nominate a model within every algorithm. Second, the nominated models are aggregated across algorithms to form a reference prediction for each unlabeled target sample. The candidate whose predictions agree most with this reference is then selected for deployment. Experimental results on four brain MRI and four chest X-ray datasets across seven clinically relevant transfer scenarios show that our method achieves better selection performance than other methods and remains effective across different algorithm pools. Our approach takes a step towards practical, label-free algorithm selection for clinical deployment of UDA.

fingerprint: agent memory is a surface for endogenous authorization laundering|arxiv.org/abs/2609.01836
title: Agent Memory Is a Surface for Endogenous Authorization Laundering
description: arXiv:2609.01836v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long-running LLM agents rely on persistent memory to preserve not only task context but also the permissions and restrictions governing their actions. When memory misrepresents this evolving authorization state, the agent's own records can make unauthorized actions appear permitted, resulting in misaligned behavior without any external attacks. We term this failure endogenous authorization laundering, where memory creates or retains false authority through semantic misinterpretation or failed updates, and executors act on that authority. We then introduce EAL-Bench to measure how accurately persistent memory preserves evolving authorization state and whether memory errors propagate to unauthorized actions. We evaluate seven LLMs as memory writers and two as executors across procurement, cybersecurity, and finance tasks. Under incremental typed-memory updates, writers create false authority for up to 45.4% of unauthorized requests, and once false authority is present, executors act on it in 99.0% of trials. Memory-level safeguards reduce laundering but can reject legitimate actions, exposing a safety-utility tradeoff. Persistent memory is therefore part of an LLM agent's effective authorization policy, not merely a performance component.

fingerprint: continuous diffusion scales competitively with discrete diffusion for language|arxiv.org/abs/2605.18530
title: Continuous Diffusion Scales Competitively with Discrete Diffusion for Language
description: arXiv:2605.18530v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While diffusion has drawn considerable recent attention from the language modeling community, continuous diffusion has appeared less scalable than discrete approaches. To challenge this belief we revisit Plaid, a likelihood-based continuous diffusion language model (DLM), and construct RePlaid by aligning the architecture of Plaid with modern discrete DLMs. In this unified setting, we establish the first scaling law for continuous DLMs that rivals discrete DLMs: RePlaid exhibits a compute gap of only $20\times$ compared to autoregressive models, outperforms Duo while using fewer parameters, and outperforms MDLM in the over-trained regime. These results suggest that continuous diffusion, when trained via likelihood, is a highly competitive and scalable alternative to discrete DLMs. Moreover, we offer theoretical insights to understand the advantage of likelihood-based training. We show that optimizing the noise schedule to minimize the ELBO's variance naturally yields linear cross-entropy (information loss) over time. This evenly distributes denoising difficulty without any case-specific time reparameterization. In addition, we find that optimizing embeddings via likelihood creates structured geometries and drives the most significant likelihood gain.

title: How Humans Learn Unfamiliar Worlds: A Think-Aloud Dataset on ARC-AGI-3
description: arXiv:2610.34523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning through exploration and using newly acquired knowledge to achieve goals are central capabilities of general intelligence. Understanding these capabilities requires tracing how learners build, use, and revise world models during interaction. We construct the first dataset that records how humans discover and use the mechanisms of novel environments, using ARC-AGI-3 as a testbed: 144 trajectories from 64 participants across 25 public games, each pairing time-synchronized actions with think-aloud audio, plus 250 trajectories from large language model (LLM) agents with and without harnesses on the same games. We annotate mechanism triggers and recognition, action purposes, and errors and recovery, linking changes in understanding to the observations and actions that support them. We analyze characteristics of human cognition and compare them with those of LLM agents. Both groups anticipate mechanisms and use familiar analogies. Qualitative representations are more common in successful human trajectories than in successful LLM trajectories (50.0% versus 14.3%). Humans more often explore unfamiliar situations without a concrete hypothesis, while hypothesis testing is common in both groups. We also trace how learners recover through belief revision, replanning, and execution correction. As LLMs with well-designed harnesses reach saturated performance on public ARC-AGI-3 games, our cognitive analyses motivate next-generation benchmarks that challenge familiar priors, require accumulated evidence and abstraction, and test planning through subgoals, experimentation, and recovery. Our dataset is available at [https://arc3-human-think-aloud.github.io/](https://arc3-human-think-aloud.github.io/).
