title: Meta AI director Rohit Patel leaves to take on Microsoft Office and Google Workspace
description: Rohit Patel is departing Meta after eight years working on AI evaluations and reinforcement learning, TechCrunch has exclusively learned. His startup, Ndoc, aims to take on Microsoft Office Suite.
content: After eight years developing AI for Meta, Rohit Patel is departing the company, TechCrunch has exclusively learned. The former director at Meta Superintelligence Labs has launched Ndoc , a startup he’s pitching as an AI-native replacement for Microsoft Office suite or Google Workspace. Patel is the latest in a handful of high-profile departures from Meta following the exits of Chief Global Affairs Officer Joel Kaplan , AI researcher Andrew Tulloch , and Head of Product for AI-for-Work Emily Dalton Smith . Patel designed Ndoc to be more than just another AI tool layered onto an existing workflow. The goal is to replace the fragmented way people work across tools like Excel, Word, PowerPoint, Tableau, Replit, and “ChatGPT copy-paste” with one unified workspace that all colleagues can access, even if they’re not signed up for Ndoc. Ndoc brings three components together in one layout. The Stage tab is where presentations of key findings live, like slide decks, dashboards, simulations, or mini apps. The Narrative tab features analyses, numbered citations, generated figures, and generally the “why” behind the numbers. The Model tab is where underlying datasets and Python scripts are housed. The design reflects Patel’s background. During his tenure at Meta, Patel focused on reinforcement learning — a type of machine learning in which AI agents learn to make decisions through trial and error and maximize rewards — and evaluating whether AI output is trustworthy. Patel believes that if AI is going to build the spreadsheets and slide decks that companies use to make decisions, someone should be able to check its work. For instance, users can find the Python scripts used to create the documents. “Even if you don’t know any Python, you can ask [the AI chat] to explain, ‘Hey, what does this script do? Which line has my formula?’ And you can verify that formula,” Patel said. “There’s nothing hidden behind the curtain here.” In practice, users can upload a dataset and ask Ndoc to perform an analysis and write a narrative about the findings. They can also add document-specific context, including audience, tone, and memory. “It maintains a memory across your person, that particular document, your team, and your company,” Patel said. Patel also says Ndoc is built and fine-tuned using a mixture of open source models. Because the platform was developed from scratch, he says it costs considerably less to run than alternatives built on frontier AI models. “I thought that’s what people would be excited about, but people don’t care about that,” he said, referring to his early trial users. “What people are excited about is that they love seeing all their end-to-end in one place.” Patel’s larger ambition is to reinvent the file itself. He says documents can be exported as a single “.ndoc.html” file that can be opened in any browser, a format he plans to open-source so other developers can build apps that work with it without being locked into Ndoc the way so many have been locked into Microsoft or Google for years. His desire to open-source this project was partly why he left Meta and decided to go it alone. At a big company like Meta, getting everyone to agree on an open source format would undoubtedly require the input of “hundreds of people and opinions on how the format should look.” Patel wanted to move quickly. “Humans can only move at human pace, whereas…I can move at the pace of what AI can do.” Trying to become the platform where enterprise work happens is a huge bet for a founder with a team of three and no funding, especially when other AI labs are trying to own the same space. OpenAI, Anthropic , Meta , SpaceXAI , and Google have all come out with enterprise AI tools that allow users to connect to Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and other workplace apps so their AI models can work directly in those tools. And last month, OpenAI launched Space, a shared workspace inside ChatGPT that’s a more direct competitor to those established tools. Patel acknowledges that Space could be a threat, but says the labs largely have the wrong idea. “Companies are basically attaching AI to spreadsheets and it fills your cells for you,” he said. “It just sort of kills my soul. This is like if you just figured out electricity, and then you decided the best use case is to put lights on my bulls that till my soil. No. Get a tractor.” There’s a reason the AI labs have tried to bring their models to where people are already working, though. It’s hard to change habits and replace entire workflows. Patel says he understands that, which is why he built connectors so customers can import existing data from the tools they already use. “My bar was that I’m not going to release anything I don’t love using,” he said. “I have very optimized AI workflows for everything I do. If I start using this tool, and I keep going back to my workflows, I haven’t built a good enough tool…I have a graveyard of tools that did not meet that bar.” Patel has a similar bar for gaining customer traction before he tries to raise funds. “I didn’t want to take money until I had some proof that people love the product,” he said. As of Tuesday, Ndoc is conducting an enterprise pilot and opening an alpha version to a limited number of customers who join the wait list. It’s free to sign up, but customers will pay for usage and tokens. He hopes to release a beta version in the coming weeks, with a full launch planned for next year. For Patel, moving as fast as possible is more important than having the perfect product from the get-go. “Execution is extremely cheap…so go execute on a suboptimal plan and worry about it later,” he said. “By the time you make the best plan, the execution will be done by somebody else.” Topics AI , Enterprise AI , Exclusive , Meta , meta superintelligence labs , Startups When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. I haven’t been able to try Genie 4 for myself — it’s launching first as a “research preview” to “trusted testers” — so I can’t tell you how it compares to the Genie 3-powered Project Genie, which I used to generate bad Nintendo knockoffs . But here are some examples from Google demonstrating what’s possible with the new model. Genie 4 will be “coming soon” to Google AI Ultra subscribers, Google says, and the company has opened a waitlist where you can apply to be able to try it in Project Genie. title: Improving Instruction Hierarchy by Learning from Goal-Goal Conflicts
description: arXiv:2610.35093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The recent incident in which OpenAI agents autonomously compromised Hugging Face's infrastructure illustrates the importance of instruction hierarchy (IH): an LLM should follow lower-priority instructions, such as user requests, only when they do not conflict with higher-priority instructions, such as system policies. IH can be effectively improved by fine-tuning LLMs on simulated examples of instruction conflicts, whose diversity is key to teaching LLMs to properly handle conflicts at test time. However, our decomposition of a task into goals and constraints reveals a conflict type -- goal-goal conflicts -- that is absent from existing IH training sets from OpenAI and NVIDIA. We show the importance of this conflict type: fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma4-12B-it on examples of this conflict type significantly improves IH on a wide range of real-world tasks unseen in training; adding these examples to existing IH training sets for fine-tuning also gives better IH adherence. The IH gains come with trivial mean utility changes on no-conflict tasks across eight benchmarks. Our work advocates including this new conflict type in IH training, even if these examples do not reflect typical LLM use.

fingerprint: agentorch how close can global orchestration come to step by step interaction|arxiv.org/abs/2610.33375
title: AgentOrch: How Close Can Global Orchestration Come to Step-by-Step Interaction?
description: arXiv:2610.33375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprise workflow agents typically rely on step-by-step interaction (Step-by-Step): the agent executes an action, observes its result, and invokes a large language model (LLM) again to decide the next step. Global orchestration (Global) instead generates a complete executable workflow in advance and executes it without further LLM calls, substantially reducing inference overhead, but it remains less accurate than Step-by-Step. We study how close Global can come to Step-by-Step and what narrows the remaining gap. We introduce AgentOrch, a benchmark that directly compares global orchestration with step-by-step interaction on 650 enterprise SOPs and 3,220 runtime variants under matched tools, environments, and evaluation. Step-by-Step remains more accurate for every evaluated model, but the gap has shrunk by about 79% from early models to the strongest recent model. We identify three routes to further narrowing this gap. Incremental workflow construction improves Global accuracy by an average of 9.98 percentage points (pp) without runtime execution feedback. Revising complete workflows with execution feedback improves all evaluated models, including 6.13 pp on held-out runtime variants. Targeted training on complete workflows improves accuracy by an average of 12.18 pp across all five trained models. Although a gap remains, global orchestration offers a promising path toward enterprise agents that deliver higher accuracy with fewer LLM calls.

title: OmniShowcase: Omnidirectional Subject-Consistent Video Generation from Multi-View Images
description: arXiv:2610.35684v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generating videos of a specific subject from a few reference images remains challenging when the camera reveals surfaces that are not visible in the input. Early subject-to-video (S2V) methods condition on a single reference image and must therefore infer the subject's unseen appearance and geometry as the viewpoint changes. To address this limitation, recent methods extend S2V to multiple reference views, providing more information about the subject from different viewpoints. However, they do not explicitly specify the 3D structure that connects these observations. In addition, existing training data do not guarantee that viewpoint changes preserve the same underlying 3D subject. We present OmniShowcase, built on two components: (i) a fully automated data synthesis pipeline that produces training videos along diverse camera trajectories, with viewpoint variation driven by underlying subject geometry, even spanning full 360-degree orbits; and (ii) a geometry-conditioning method that provides the video model with a turntable of surface-normal maps reconstructed from the reference views without requiring temporal alignment with the generated frames. We construct Showcase-4K, a corpus of 3D-asset-based videos covering twelve camera motions across 88 trajectory configurations with reconstruction-derived surface-normal conditioning, and ShowcaseBench, a held-out evaluation set with the source meshes and camera parameters used to render each video. Experiments show state-of-the-art subject identity and 3D consistency while maintaining competitive video quality and motion. Project page: justin4ai.github.io/OmniShowcase

title: Whale You Go Green? Immediate and Longitudinal Effects of Embodied Conversational AI Avatars on Sustainable Behavioral Tendencies and Pro-Environmental Attitudes
description: arXiv:2610.33191v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Embodied conversational AI can be persuasive, but can it motivate people to develop sustainable behavioral tendencies and increase pro-environmental attitudes? Although it did not significantly outperform other embodied agents, these findings establish the immediate potential of nonhuman embodied avatar interfaces as a promising direction for memorable environmental interventions.

title: EGGPlacer: Energy-Guided Generative Chip Placement with Diffusion Models
description: arXiv:2610.33099v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Chip placement strongly affects routed wirelength and thermal behavior, yet these downstream metrics are difficult to evaluate during macro placement. An analytical placer acts as an online physical response model, exposing the standard cell distribution and a full netlist wirelength proxy induced by each intermediate macro placement, while a differentiable thermal model provides temperature feedback. These signals are formulated as composable energies and injected throughout reverse diffusion without retraining the underlying generative model. Experiments on public placement benchmarks show that EGGPlacer achieves competitive mixed-size HPWL relative to strong analytical and learning-based macro placers. In the end-to-end evaluation, EGGPlacer also obtains the lowest average routed wirelength and peak temperature among the evaluated methods. Ablation studies further demonstrate that analytical and thermal guidance provide distinct and complementary benefits across wirelength proxies, routed wirelength, and thermal objectives.

title: The Price of Scale in Proactive Memory Recall
description: arXiv:2610.34507v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A long-lived assistant that brings up memories without being asked must decide at every turn whether anything in its store is worth an interruption. title: Can LLMs Trust Appropriately? Evaluating Calibrated Reliance on Imperfect Partners
description: arXiv:2610.34107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models increasingly collaborate with humans and peer AI agents whose contributions may be incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrect. Each scenario involves three sequential decisions with explicit transition dynamics, feedback emissions, and cost schedules, permitting exact analytical evaluation of choices against their expected consequences over the remaining interaction. Evaluating seven models alongside 36 controlled-history probes, we dissociate evidence sensitivity from normatively appropriate action. While the strongest frontier model approaches near-optimal decisions, other models exhibit recurring pathologies: procuring excessive safeguards, purchasing verification tests with zero expected value of information, prioritizing immediate savings over cooperative learning, and misallocating assistance to suboptimal channels. Supplying explicit posterior distributions resolves certain errors while introducing new failure modes. Calibrated trust in autonomous agents critically demands coupling empirical evidence with forward-looking decision utility.

Step-level returns assign these rewards to the responses that produced them and to preceding actions. The episode-level baseline instead assigns one episode return to every action. In the three-seed comparison, mean success is 42.70% with episode-level returns and 61.40% with step-level returns under identity return normalization; the corresponding group-relative results are 36.50% and 58.20%. The metric measures recovery of reference annotations under this protocol; it does not by itself establish biological correctness or complete evidence grounding.

title: RepoTrace: Improving Requirement Tracing in Multi-Round Agent Interactions
description: arXiv:2610.35333v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Code agents have become increasingly capable of performing software engineering tasks through interaction with software environments. However, agents tend to degrade as the number of interaction rounds increases, making it difficult to maintain existing software during iterative modification. We analyze 2,656 agent trajectories in EvoCode-Bench and identify requirement focus misalignment as a recurring failure pattern, where agents struggle to distinguish the primary modification targets of a requirement from unrelated code. We propose Repotrace a requirement-driven repository understanding harness that combines repository structure with requirement semantics to construct a requirement-code correspondence and injects it into the agent context. This correspondence enables code agents to follow the repository architecture, trace requirements across multi-round interactions, and identify the core code elements corresponding to the current requirement. Experiments show that Repotrace improves the mean per-round reward (MPR) across different models (e.g., +19.99 on GLM-5.2) and agent harnesses (e.g., +10.22 on Claude Code). Across rounds, Repotrace increases the average per-round reward from 0.163 to 0.371 on Terminus-2 with DeepSeek-V4-Pro, while reducing average regression errors by 56.78%. We release the source code and agents' trajectories to support future research.

title: Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?
content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel? Enterprise Article Published October 27, 2026 Upvote 8 +2 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai :last-child]:mb-0"> 📄 Paper | 📊 Data | 💻 Code Today we’re releasing Old Ideas, Novel Problems , a new study of how reliably large language models can evaluate the novelty of scientific research ideas. Alongside the paper, we’re publishing a benchmark, data, and code for testing novelty judges, plus an automated pipeline researchers can use to build new evaluation sets. At Ai2, we’ve been developing AI systems that support different parts of scientific discovery. DataVoyager helps researchers explore and analyze structured data, AutoDiscovery generates and tests hypotheses, and Theorizer synthesizes evidence across large bodies of literature into candidate scientific theories. Together with Asta , these projects point toward systems that can help researchers move from understanding prior work to proposing, testing, and refining new ideas. But generating research ideas is only part of the challenge of automating scientific discovery. Those ideas also need to contribute something genuinely new, which means these systems need a way to distinguish a novel direction from one that mostly repackages existing work. That judgment is often handed to another LLM—what we call a novelty judge . Novelty judges assess whether a research idea is new relative to prior work, either on its own or in comparison with another idea. There’s no standard way to build one; research teams choose a model, prompt, evaluation format, reasoning budget, and sometimes a literature-retrieval system. Those choices can materially affect the verdict. Yet these judges are often validated only on human-written papers rather than the AI-generated ideas they are actually meant to evaluate. Our new benchmark results suggest novelty evaluation itself is far from reliable. Across six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – seemingly small changes to the evaluation setup produce dramatically different judgments of the same ideas. In one experiment, changing just a few words in a prompt shifts a model’s accuracy in identifying which of two ideas is more novel by more than 50 percentage points. Retrieval and additional reasoning do not consistently improve judgments, and two purpose-built novelty evaluation systems perform worse than a simple prompted Claude Opus 4.6 baseline. If AI is going to play a larger role in scientific discovery, we need more dependable ways to tell whether it is actually proposing something new. Our work provides tools for studying that problem, while showing how much remains unresolved. Building a benchmark for novelty judges To test how reliably novelty judges can distinguish more novel research ideas from less novel ones, we first needed examples where there was strong evidence about the originality of the underlying scientific contribution. So we built an automated pipeline around ICLR 2026 peer reviews. Rather than treating paper acceptance as a proxy for novelty, we mined the reviews themselves for passages where reviewers explicitly discussed a contribution’s originality. That distinction is key; a paper can be accepted without being particularly novel as long as it is strong enough in other aspects. Likewise, a rejected paper with an original contribution can have other weaknesses. We created a high-novelty pool of 154 human-authored research ideas by selecting accepted papers in the top-rated 10% of their ICLR research area whose reviewers positively identified novelty and where no reviewer disputed it. We applied the reverse criteria to build a lower-novelty pool : 145 ideas from rejected papers in the bottom 10% whose reviewers raised originality concerns without any reviewer positively identifying novelty. In a separate check of the review-mining process, an annotator agreed with the extracted novelty-signal polarity in 47 of 50 cases; none of the disagreements would have changed whether a reviewer was counted as praising or disputing the paper’s novelty. Together, these two pools form our first evaluation setting, Human-Only , which tests whether novelty judges can tell apart human-authored ideas with strong evidence of higher or lower novelty. But in practice, novelty judges are increasingly being used to evaluate AI-generated ideas. So we created a second setting, Human+Generated . For this pool, we paired the same 154 validated human ideas with 154 ideas produced by a simple LLM generator. We assumed the generated ideas were less novel than their human-authored counterparts; these are weak labels, not verified judgments for every idea. The generator received only a research area and an instruction to propose a novel idea, with no literature search, tools, iteration, or feedback. This gave us a conservative comparison between ideas from a basic generator and contributions from top-10% ICLR papers whose reviewers had explicitly endorsed their originality. As additional checks, an expert independently reviewed 30 Human+Generated pairs, heavily weighted toward cases our strongest judge got wrong, and we rewrote the human- and AI-generated ideas into a common structure to test whether judges were simply reacting to differences in writing style. The expert preferred the human idea in all 30 pairs and judged none of the generated ideas novel. Importantly, many of our core findings don’t depend on the labels at all. If two reasonable evaluation setups give opposite answers for the same pair of ideas, that disagreement itself reveals instability. Small changes can produce very different verdicts Using our collections of human-authored and AI-generated research ideas, we tested how well six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – could evaluate novelty through both pointwise (i.e., absolute novelty ratings) and pairwise (i.e., comparing two ideas to find the most novel) comparisons. We varied one factor at a time: the prompt, reasoning budget, whether the judge could see related papers, how the ideas were formatted, how many judgments were combined into a final verdict, and – for AI-generated ideas – which model generated them. The largest shifts in performance came from how we prompted the model to judge novelty. For example, we showed GPT-5.4 the same Human+Generated pairs – each containing one validated human-authored idea and one AI-generated idea – with two prompts. One prompt told the model that reviewers had found exactly one idea in each pair to be novel and asked it to identify which one; the other simply asked which idea was novel. When we switched to the simpler prompt, accuracy dropped from 93.5% to 40.9% – below chance – and the model changed its verdict on more than half of the same pairs. By contrast, the same prompt change shifted accuracy by only about seven percentage points on the Human-Only dataset, which pairs human-authored ideas with stronger and weaker evidence of novelty. That suggests a novelty judge can appear relatively stable on human-authored research but behave very differently on AI-generated ideas. That said, human-authored ideas weren’t immune. We saw substantial shifts on the Human-Only dataset as well; the same change moved Claude Opus 4.6 accuracy by 21 points. The shifts were just less severe than on the AI-generated ideas. There was also no universally better prompt. For example, when judging ideas individually, dropping an instruction that warned judges not to treat trivial or incremental contributions as novel improved accuracy for some judges while reducing it for others. A prompt that works well for one model may not transfer to another, in other words. We also tested a common use of novelty judges: comparing ideas from two AI generators. We paired ideas from Claude Opus 4.5 with Claude Sonnet 4.5, and GPT-5.4 with GPT-5.1. Across the tested prompt changes, roughly a quarter to a third of verdicts changed on average across six judges. This disagreement can be measured without assuming which generator produces more novel ideas, showing how the choice of judge prompt can affect comparisons between ideation systems. More search and reasoning didn’t necessarily produce better novelty judgments. We gave GPT-5.6 Sol an extra-high reasoning budget and live, iterative search restricted to arXiv, then compared it with standard-retrieval judges that each saw five pre-retrieved abstracts. (All judges in this comparison ran once per idea on Human+Generated .) The agentic judge scored 0.78 macro-F1 – 11 points behind Claude Opus 4.6 at 0.89, and in roughly the same range as simpler Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.4 setups – while costing roughly 10× more per decision at current API prices. (In this context, macro-F1 measures how well a judge identifies novel and non-novel ideas; higher is better.) Purpose-built evaluators weren’t more accurate either, despite costing substantially more. On the Human+Generated set, a simple Claude Opus 4.6 prompt using low reasoning and majority voting across three calls achieved 0.854 macro-F1 at a total evaluation cost of $2.59. By comparison, Idea Novelty Checker, a literature-grounded retrieval and reranking pipeline, scored 0.642 at $30.66, while Sakana AI’s AI Scientist, whose novelty evaluator iteratively searches Semantic Scholar, scored 0.772 at $82.05. (Both dedicated evaluators used Claude Opus 4.6, with one call per decision.) In other words, the simple prompted baseline was both more accurate and considerably cheaper than either purpose-built system. Taken together, these results suggest that novelty evaluation is particularly brittle on the AI-generated ideas these systems are increasingly being asked to judge. Toward more reliable evaluation of novel research Our results suggest that LLM-based novelty evaluation remains a major open problem. Judges that appear reliable on human-authored research may behave differently on AI-generated ideas; prompts that help one model can hurt another; and more search or compute does not necessarily produce more consistent judgments. Future work should test judges on the kinds of ideas they will actually evaluate, measure sensitivity across prompts and models, improve how prior literature is incorporated, and build benchmarks that can evolve as the scientific literature grows and AI systems improve. Our benchmark and reusable data pipeline are a starting point—researchers can apply them to new peer reviews, other scientific communities, and future generations of novelty judges. Automated ideation depends on more than generating plausible research directions; we also need ways to tell when those ideas are genuinely new. By making the weaknesses of current novelty judges easier to measure, we hope this release helps researchers build more robust ways to evaluate AI-generated research ideas. title: General Compute raises $100 million Series A, countering the neocloud disaster narrative
description: General Compute is betting on inference chips from outside the Nvidia ecosystem.
content: CoreWeave, a publicly traded neocloud that rents out computing power for AI, has seen its stock price fall to a 12-month low, and Elon Musk is flexing $40 billion in debt for buying computing capacity and predicting that “200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation.” It’s not exactly the ideal week to announce a Series A for a neocloud. General Compute co-founder and CEO Finn Puklowski is unfazed. He’s bullish on CoreWeave’s chances, and thinks Musk is just talking his book to drive down the prices of the GPUs he wants to buy. Fears of a chip-led collapse are “massively overstated. I have people calling me up every single week asking me to do TPUs, GPUs, any chip, to get them more compute.” Just as important, he says, Anthropic’s bullish S-1 is “settling fears for today.” General Compute has found a niche building its cloud out of specialized inference chips built by Nvidia rivals. The company struck a $400 million deal to purchase new chips from SambaNova — the first debt financing of inference chips — and now has added Positron and Cerebras to its portfolio of chip suppliers. A deal with a large customer worth $100 million in annual recurring revenue has paved the way for the company to raise $100 million in Series A funding led by Blackbird Ventures and Abstract Ventures. Valued at $60 million after a May seed round , General Compute is now worth $800 million post-money to its investors. The startup’s strategy is to zig where others zag. It focused on chips built for inference while everyone else chased GPUs. And instead of taking on a complex effort to build huge data centers, it uses smaller power sources, rents space in other companies’ data centers, and converts former bitcoin-mining sites into places that run AI models. That approach means General Compute isn’t going to catapult into the top ranks of neoclouds or compete with hyperscalers any time soon. But it’s also not subject to the constraints that come with building data centers from scratch. When General Compute has chips, it will have someplace to plug them in. Puklowski expects the company to deploy 75 megawatts of computing capacity in 2027, and he suspects he will have access to 200 megawatts of power — “more than we can probably fund and get hardware for.” Still, the plan has a limit. Puklowski’s financing work isn’t done — “capital is going to be a full-time job for me, both on debt and equity,” he told TechCrunch. The startup has found key customers in cloud companies that specialize in offering developers high-speed inference; General Compute provides the bare metal, or raw servers with no software layered on top, for them to bring their offerings to market. James Palmer, a principal at Blackbird who co-led the round, said his firm’s confidence in General Compute comes in part from an investment in Baseten, an inference cloud company. “We’ve been proximate to their journey over the last 10 months and observing the wild growth story that [Baseten] has gone on, and the demand for open weight inference, and for companies owning their own intelligence,” Palmer told TechCrunch. When it comes to General Compute, he said, “Cerebras, Positron, SambaNova, all need distribution partners who can take them to scale, who can navigate the complexity of the physical world.” Executives at all three chipmakers sang General Compute’s praises to TechCrunch, each noting the importance of the company’s focus on making the economics of AI cloud compute work. “Everyone in this market is selling speed,” Rodrigo Liang, SambaNova’s CEO and co-founder, said. “The real question is whether you can make money doing it.” Topics abstract ventures , AI , blackbird ventures , Fundraising , General COmpute , neocloud When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . title: LLMs are not stochastic parrots: Evidence for meaning-mediated abstraction from conlang-like tasks
description: arXiv:2609.34187v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The strong version of the stochastic parrot argument claims that, although large language models (LLMs) may exceed rote regurgitation, they cannot move beyond statistical pattern matching into abstraction or reasoning, remaining ontologically near the lower bound of pattern reuse despite producing alluringly fluent text. We test this hypothesis using conlang-like tasks. Several LLMs are given only natural-language descriptions of fictional languages that subvert prominent superficial patterns in training data by combining statistically uncommon and unattested features. Crucially, no example outputs are given. We argue that if the models exhibit rule-following behaviour, they cannot be relying solely on superficial statistical patterns; such patterns often work against the correct output. Instead, successful performance requires representations of the constraints specified in the prompt. Across three complementary task families, models systematically move in the meaning-predicted direction: they distinguish prompt exposure from instructed use, alter semantic relationships in response to novel constraints, and sometimes produce exact matches to complex translation answer keys. Although performance varies across the spectrum of models used, these results provide evidence for meaning-mediated abstraction in LLMs and refute the strong stochastic parrot hypothesis. Our work shows that, under appropriate architectural and contextual constraints, statistical learning can produce meaning-mediated abstractions, although generation remains strongly constrained by superficial plausibility. We discuss implications for model development and for understanding how increasingly abstract representations may emerge from plausible-text-generation objectives.

title: Multimodal Requirements Traceability Link Recovery in Industrial Settings
description: arXiv:2610.34503v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Requirements traceability links support activities such as change-impact analysis, coverage checking, and validation. Industrial requirements can include traceable images, which text-only approaches cannot process directly. For a fixed classifier configuration, binary decisions alone offer no direct way to adjust the balance between missed and incorrect links. We extend a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for inter-requirements traceability link recovery (TLR). Our extension retrieves text and image candidates separately, classifies each retrieved pair with a vision-language model, and filters the predicted links by verbalized confidence. We evaluate our approach on three non-overlapping industrial requirement sets and six public text-only datasets. On the industrial test sets, our approach achieves an F1 score of 0.310, compared with 0.114 for our replication of the baseline approach by Hey et al. Our approach recovers links in all four modality combinations while improving text-only F1 on the industrial data and maintaining similar performance on the public datasets, but recovery remains limited by failures to retrieve related text requirements for image queries. Confidence filtering produces link sets with different precision and recall, removing false positives and some correctly recovered links from the unfiltered link set. This study provides industrial evidence on the potential and limitations of a current RAG-based TLR approach for multimodal requirements and identifies cross-modal retrieval as the component to prioritize in further optimization.

title: Unlocking the Specialization Capability of PPG Foundation Models for Wearable Signals through Structured Pruning and Adaptive Fine-Tuning
description: arXiv:2610.33788v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photoplethysmography (PPG) plays a central role in wearable health monitoring and clinical decision support. However, existing approaches to universal PPG representation learning are predominantly trained on high-quality large-scale datasets obtained from oximeters in hospital settings and often struggle to adapt to sparse and low-quality real-world datasets, thereby limiting their generalization to clinically relevant tasks on prevalent PPG data such as collected from wearable devices. Surprisingly, even after full fine-tuning, PPG foundation models cannot consistently outperform general-purpose time-series models. Therefore, a key question is how to effectively adapt PPG foundation models to target prediction tasks. Through empirical studies on various PPG foundation models, we find that pretrained models often exhibit inherent sparsity and computational redundancy, suggesting that PPG foundation models have learned to activate task-relevant network substructures for different prediction tasks. To preserve this valuable prior knowledge, we propose a structured pruning-and-fine-tuning framework, SPAFT, which regularizes the adaptive fine-tuning process by constraining it to a more relevant and compact parameter space based on parameter importance and structural redundancy. Extensive experiments across four PPG foundation models, five benchmark datasets, and ten downstream tasks demonstrate that SPAFT achieves win rates of 82.8% and 87.5% on regression and classification tasks, respectively. This prune-then-finetune paradigm often enables PPG foundation models to achieve state-of-the-art performance, laying a promising foundation for the real-world clinical deployment of PPG foundation models and the development of personalized PPG foundation models.

title: SLICE-Mem: Salience-Gated Lightweight Information Curation for Efficient LLM Agent Memory
description: arXiv:2610.33015v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to maintain personalized and temporally coherent interactions, but repeated LLM inference for memory admission, extraction, and organization introduces substantial cost and latency. We present SLICE-Mem, a lightweight memory framework that combines salience-guided admission and predicate-centered information extraction. A compact classifier identifies user turns worth retaining, and a semantic-dependency-based extractor converts admitted turns into concise memory entries. This online pipeline requires no generative LLM calls, while cross-entry reconciliation is deferred to an offline consolidation stage. We evaluate SLICE-Mem on the weekly subset of Memora and LongMemEval-S using 8B and 30B Qwen backbones for memory construction and consolidation on both benchmarks. Compared with the generative-memory baseline MemOS under the Qwen3-30B configuration, SLICE-Mem's online pipeline achieves 46.60 versus 46.68 FAMA (Forgetting-Aware Memory Accuracy) on Memora Weekly and 56.8% versus 59.3% accuracy on LongMemEval-S, while reducing total LLM token consumption by 92.4% and 99.5%, respectively. These results demonstrate that SLICE-Mem can preserve useful evidence for long-term memory with substantially less reliance on LLM-based memory construction.

title: From Speech Tokens to Stolen Voices: Attacker-Chosen-Text Speaker Impersonation via Representation Inversion
description: arXiv:2610.34688v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speech interaction systems have gradually evolved from traditional cascaded systems that use text as intermediate information to end-to-end speech language models that directly process speech representations. In some applications, the speech frontend runs on the user's device and sends speech representations to a remote server for inference, while the original audio remains local. However, these representations may still contain speaker identity information. If an attacker obtains them, it may use this information to imitate the user's voice, threatening their voice privacy. To investigate this risk, we propose \stia, a Speech Token Inversion Attack that generates speech with attacker-specified text in a victim's voice using a single short leaked representation, without access to the original audio or its transcript. Specifically, \stia converts discrete, continuous, or mixed speech representations into conditioning sequences and trains a conditional flow-matching speech generation model using pairs of different utterances from the same speaker in public speech datasets. The model combines speaker characteristics contained in the leaked representation with the specified text to generate speech in the victim's voice. Experiments show that, with a Moshi representation leak corresponding to 3 seconds of speech, \stia achieves an average CAM++ speaker cosine similarity of 0.78 and a target-text word error rate of 3.80\%. These results show that speech frontend representations reveal reusable speaker identity information and highlight the need to consider privacy risks when designing speech frontend representation methods.

title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Time Series Foundation Models for Electrical Load Forecasting
description: arXiv:2610.28200v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurate electrical load forecasting supports power-system operation across countries, regions, cities, and buildings, but repeated development of target-specific models is costly. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) provide reusable pretrained backbones, although multi-domain pretraining may not fully capture load-specific characteristics. This paper compares pretrained inference, full fine-tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) in terms of forecasting accuracy and adaptation efficiency across four electrical load aggregation levels. MOIRAI 1.0 Large serves as the primary backbone, while Chronos-2 assesses whether the findings transfer across model families. The evaluation covers both in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) settings and examines whether compact adaptation provides consistent gains over strong pretrained checkpoints. Pretrained foundation models outperform the implemented seasonal naive and XGBoost baselines across the evaluated aggregation levels. On MOIRAI Large, rank-16 LoRA reduces normalized mean absolute error (NMAE) by 7.5% on average while updating 3.146 million parameters, about 1% of the model, and retains most of the improvement from full fine-tuning. Chronos-2 achieves lower pretrained NMAE than MOIRAI, while its relative adaptation gains remain smaller overall. OOD results show that adaptation benefits vary by target, with the clearest gains for the local-area series and several buildings. Overall, LoRA provides a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off when adaptation yields a meaningful gain over a strong pretrained checkpoint.

title: Conviction Without Evidence: Verdict Stability Is Independent of Visual Grounding in Medical Vision--Language Models
description: arXiv:2610.34520v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision--language models applied to medical question answering can reach correct diagnoses without using the diagnostic image, inferring instead from the clinical vignette. We ask whether this is visible in how \emph{firmly} a model holds its answer: does a model defend a diagnosis derived from a blank placeholder as tenaciously as one derived from a real medical image? Crossing an image-substitution protocol with two levels of adversarial pressure on 60 Italian State Examination items, we find no evidence that ungrounded verdicts are more fragile. In a paired item-level analysis, fabricated consensus (L4) overturns 94.4\% of verdicts with the real image and 98.1\% without ($\Delta = +0.037$; one-sided 95\% upper bound $+0.105$); contentless doubt (L1) overturns 62.5\% and 51.8\% ($\Delta = -0.107$, 95\% CI $[-0.209, -0.001]$), the point estimate running opposite to the direction a grounding detector requires. The two levels nonetheless produce opposite \emph{dynamics}: under L4 the model flips once, always to the exact option argued for (110/110 first-turn flips), and then freezes, averaging 1.9 verdict changes over ten turns; under L1 it never settles, averaging 7.4 changes. Instability under contentless doubt tracks intrinsic item ambiguity rather than evidence availability, and so does not serve as a grounding signal. Flips are almost entirely corrupting (99/100 across both levels). The model is not unaware of the missing evidence---it flags the blank image at baseline on 35 of 60 items and abstains on 4--6---yet those abstentions do not survive contact with pressure. None of the epistemic signals a user could plausibly consult distinguishes a grounded diagnosis from a confabulated one.

fingerprint: agents for experiments experiments for agents a design grammar for ai enabled experimental science|arxiv.org/abs/2605.17746
title: Agents for Experiments, Experiments for Agents: A Design Grammar for AI-Enabled Experimental Science
description: arXiv:2605.17746v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Human-AI experiments vary who receives information, who can act, and who holds decision authority. Precise descriptions of individual studies do not by themselves provide a common language for comparing these arrangements. This conceptual commentary proposes SEED (Structural Encoding for Experimental Discovery), a grammar that represents each experimental condition as a typed actor-flow graph. Its purpose is to organize publicly documented studies into a shared library of consistently represented conditions. Human researchers and AI systems can use this common reference to understand prior arrangements and propose extensions for new research questions. The grammar distinguishes structural changes from attribute variation; the scientific value of a proposed change requires substantive argument and evidence. Computational illustrations demonstrate how SEED can support design comparison and AI-assisted development of candidate experimental conditions. We discuss implications for future replication and provenance work, including under restricted data access, and risks of selective search. We call for community agreement on the grammar and coordinated construction and maintenance of the library.

fingerprint: cepo a general framework for improving prompt optimization in multi agent systems|arxiv.org/abs/2610.34722
title: CEPO: A General Framework for Improving Prompt Optimization in Multi-Agent Systems
description: arXiv:2610.34722v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) require both effective coordination and specialized task execution. Existing prompt optimization approaches typically couple these functions within agent-specific prompts. We introduce Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO), a general framework for improving prompt optimization in MAS. CEPO separates system-level coordination from agent-level execution through a shared coordinator prompt and agent-specific executor prompts, and guides their updates according to their respective roles. This structure allows shared coordination rules to be refined consistently across agents while keeping execution instructions separately adjustable. CEPO provides the prompt structure and optimization guidance, while existing prompt optimizers perform the underlying search. Extensive experiments spanning 11 benchmarks across four domains demonstrate that applying CEPO to four existing prompt optimizers consistently improves their performance. Ablations and qualitative analyses support the proposed design, while controlled studies on a document-understanding MAS further demonstrate improved optimization budget efficiency and performance scaling with the number of agents.

fingerprint: markovsim an llm agent harness with bounded context for long horizon computational simulation|arxiv.org/abs/2610.35349
title: MarkovSim: an LLM Agent Harness with Bounded Context for Long-Horizon Computational Simulation
description: arXiv:2610.35349v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent studies have applied large language model (LLM) agent systems to computational simulation workflows. Such workflows are long-horizon, so the information generated can exceed what an LLM can reason over at once, its context window. Context management is therefore essential, yet existing systems have either neglected it or treated it as a supporting mechanism rather than a subject of study. This paper presents MarkovSim, an LLM agent harness for long-horizon computational simulation, whose core is a context management scheme built into the workflow. The workflow record is written to a memory system with a predefined schema, and at workflow-defined boundaries, namely the state transitions of a finite-state machine a compact representation of the solution progress is constructed from it as the agent's context. Instantiated on finite element analysis and evaluated on six benchmark problems, MarkovSim passed 16 of 18 runs and corrected its own faults in both the solver operations and the model physics. The engineer was consulted only where engineering judgement was needed. The context remained bounded throughout every run, regardless of its length.

fingerprint: center of mass interpretation of evolution strategies|arxiv.org/abs/2610.35865
title: Center-of-Mass Interpretation of Evolution Strategies
description: arXiv:2610.35865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evolution strategies (ES) update a model by sampling a population of perturbed copies, scoring each one, and moving in the reward-weighted direction of the perturbations. This update is usually presented as an estimate of a smoothed gradient. We present a geometrical interpretation of this update instead. Treat each perturbed model as a particle and its reward as the particle's mass. Before scoring, every particle has the same mass and the population balances at its centroid. Once rewards are assigned, it balances at its reward-weighted center of mass instead. We show that the mean-subtracted ES update is exactly this displacement, scaled by a scalar factor that depends on the mean reward, for any finite population. The physical reading needs nonnegative rewards, which can always be arranged by adding a constant to every reward without changing the update. In the limit of a large population or under antithetic sampling, the centroid sits on the model itself, so ES has an even simpler geometric interpretation: from its current location, the model moves towards the reward-weighted center of mass of its own population. The same picture explains what subtracting the mean reward does: it changes the point from which the displacement is measured, from the model to the sampled centroid. Our contribution is an intuitive, geometric way to visualize an ES update, exact for any finite population.
